desc:
The array digits contains values from 0 to 9. A non-empty subarray is palindrome-friendly if its elements can be reordered into a sequence that reads the same forwards and backwards. Count the palindrome-friendly subarrays (different positions count separately).

Equivalently, in the subarray at most one value occurs an odd number of times.

digits = [1, 1, 2]
subarrays: [1], [1], [2], [1, 1], [1, 1, 2]
result = 5     ([1, 2] is not palindrome-friendly)
constraints: The answer is at most n(n + 1) / 2 and fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Only the parity (odd or even) of each value's count matters, not the counts themselves.
Encode the parities of the ten values as a 10-bit mask, flipping one bit per element. The mask of a subarray is the XOR of two prefix masks.

A subarray is palindrome-friendly if its mask is 0 or has exactly one bit set. For each prefix mask m, add the number of earlier prefixes with mask m and with mask m ^ (1 << b) for each of the 10 bits.
editorial: Let mask_j be the parity mask after the first j elements (bit d is 1 if digit d occurred an odd number of times). The subarray between prefixes i < j has mask mask_i ^ mask_j. It can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when that mask has at most one set bit.

So for every j we count earlier prefixes i such that mask_i = mask_j (subarray mask 0) or mask_i = mask_j ^ (1 << b) for one of the 10 bits. Keep a frequency array of size 1024 (seeded with the empty prefix, mask 0 once). Each element does 11 lookups, so the time is O(11 n) = O(n) and the space is O(210). The same trick generalises to any alphabet of size A with O(n A) time and O(2A) space.
solution:
def countPalindromeSubarrays(digits):
    freq = [0] * 1024
    freq[0] = 1
    mask = 0
    total = 0
    for d in digits:
        mask ^= 1 << d
        total += freq[mask]
        for b in range(10):
            total += freq[mask ^ (1 << b)]
        freq[mask] += 1
    return total
